post.text:
UP TO SPEED. ⚡

The last 24 hours in transhumanism:
- DeepMind's AI agents found faster quantum algorithms, all proved
- A rare muscle-wasting disease gets its first approved drug
- 1 in 4 students used AI for mental-health support (survey)
- Robots that stop when unsure
post.alt: A 3-minute video recap of the last 24 hours in transhumanism (24 Nov 2026): DeepMind's proof-checked quantum algorithms, the first approved drug for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, a speech brain implant going portable with Nvidia, Claude Ship, Meta's superintelligence warning, Thomas Nagel on AI consciousness, air pollution and dementia, leukaemia's early start, digital brain twins, older drivers in South Australia, what makes singles happy, students using AI for mental-health support, Australia's peptide inquiry, AI robot safety, a folding drone, a Chernobyl fungus against nerve agents and robots that stop when unsure, with captions, sources and screenshots of the articles.

stories.title: Google DeepMind's AI agent teams found faster quantum algorithms and proved each one
stories.summary: Teams of Gemini 4 agents improved known quantum algorithms, cutting a fusion-simulation circuit's cost 11.8x and speeding one routine 290x, each result proved in the Lean proof checker. It's Google's own paper, and the circuits still need more than early error-corrected quantum computers will offer.

predictions.note: Gemini 4 agent teams cut a fusion-simulation circuit's cost 11.8x and sped one routine 290x, each proved in Lean; one company's result.

stories.title: The FDA approves the first drug for a limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
stories.summary: BridgeBio's Welgemda (ribitol), a twice-daily oral drug, is the first approved treatment for any form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, for type 2I/R9. In its phase 3 trial of 112 people, walking speed rose 0.14 m/s on the drug as it fell 0.12 m/s on placebo; the approval rests on 12-month interim data.
stories.evidence: Approved by the FDA; interim phase 3 data

stories.title: Paradromics and Nvidia aim to shrink a speech brain implant's cart of electronics to a box
stories.summary: Mary, a Michigan woman with motor neuron disease, speaks through a dime-sized Paradromics implant with more than 400 electrodes, its signals decoded by AI on a cart of electronics. With Nvidia hardware and software, the company aims to fit that on her wheelchair within a year.

predictions.note: A speech-decoding brain implant is set to move from a cart of electronics to a box on the user's wheelchair, using Nvidia hardware.

stories.title: Anthropic's Claude can now fix failing code checks and approve routine changes
stories.summary: Claude Ship adds two beta agents for Claude Team and Enterprise customers on GitHub: PR Steward fixes failing checks, merge conflicts and review feedback, and Claude Approvals can approve routine changes where a team's policy allows.

predictions.note: Claude's new agents fix failing code checks and can approve routine changes where a team's policy allows; a beta launch by one company.

stories.title: Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang says superintelligence is arriving
stories.summary: Alexandr Wang posted on X that 'superintelligence is arriving' and that how humanity acts over the next year 'will have great consequence', warning against a 'handover' of society to AI and calling for urgent safety, alignment and security work. It's an opinion, not a study.

stories.title: Philosopher Thomas Nagel says fluent language doesn't make an AI conscious
stories.summary: Thomas Nagel, famous for his 1974 essay on what it's like to be a bat, told WIRED that producing language isn't enough for an AI to count as conscious, and criticised AI welfare work at Anthropic and elsewhere. Anthropic's view is that we can't yet be sure either way.

stories.title: Dirtier air is linked to more dementia, and in mice it rewired brain immune cells
stories.summary: In about 500,000 UK adults followed up to 14 years, those in the most polluted third were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer's or a related dementia. In mice, five months of polluted air reprogrammed brain immune cells and harmed memory. The human part is a link, not proof.
stories.evidence: Observational study plus a mouse study

stories.title: Leukaemia's first mutation often arises before age 20, decades before diagnosis
stories.summary: Using blood stored for up to 15 years before diagnosis, Cambridge and UCL researchers found that in two-thirds of 47 women who later developed acute myeloid leukaemia, the first driver mutation arose before age 20. A single dominant clone showed up years early in at least a third: a possible warning sign.

stories.title: Digital twins of 6,986 brains model ageing, dementia and the environment
stories.summary: Researchers built biophysical models of 6,986 people's brains, aged 18 to 100 in 16 countries, each tuned to the person's MRI. Age, dementia and surroundings such as air pollution and democratic conditions were linked to how the simulated brains behaved: associations, not causes.

stories.title: Older South Australian drivers' crash rate fell after medical checks were relaxed
stories.summary: After South Australia swapped a compulsory medical check at 70 for a self-assessment at 75 in 2015, injury crashes per licensed older driver fell and medical licence suspensions rose, an Adelaide University review of 1997-2023 data found. Drivers aged 70+ grew from about 125,000 to 200,000.

stories.title: Singles who feel free are more satisfied with life, in five countries
stories.summary: In a survey of 5,017 singles aged 30 and over in the US, UK, Japan, Mexico and Spain, a sense of freedom and independence went with higher life satisfaction, and 'singlism', stigma for being single, with lower. It shows links rather than causes.

stories.title: One in four Bath students used AI for mental-health support
stories.summary: In a survey of 2,020 University of Bath students, one in four had used generative AI for mental-health support in six months, including more than a third of those with very low wellbeing. It measured use, not benefit; the researchers flag wrong advice, privacy and crisis responses as risks.

stories.title: Australia orders an inquiry into unapproved peptides sold online
stories.summary: Health Minister Mark Butler ordered a parliamentary inquiry into peptides sold online and through telehealth for weight loss, anti-ageing and muscle. Monthly NSW hospital visits linked to unapproved peptides rose from 5 in July 2025 to 217 in September 2026.

stories.title: Top AI models steering robots often caused harm in tests, and a safety harness helped
stories.summary: The RoboRisk benchmark put six frontier models through 92 simulated and 13 real robot tasks and found they 'typically produced high rates of harmful outcomes'. A safety harness called LEASH cut harm for all six without ending it. It's a preprint, not yet peer reviewed.

stories.title: A drone folds its springy arms to squeeze through gaps about half its width
stories.summary: Its spring-loaded, 3D-printed arms fold on contact, shrinking it 55%, from 31.3 cm to 14.1 cm, with no folding motors, and it flew through a 15 cm gap at about 2 m/s. It's a preprint and a prototype.

stories.title: A pigment like a Chernobyl fungus's breaks down a nerve-agent stand-in
stories.summary: Researchers made allomelanin, the pore-filled pigment of a mould that thrives at Chernobyl, into tiny spheres with zirconium clusters; the best broke down half of a nerve-agent stand-in in under 10 minutes. The aim is protective gear that destroys toxic chemicals; so far it's lab work.
stories.evidence: Lab study with a chemical stand-in

stories.title: Munich's robots stop when they're unsure, then learn the new move from a person
stories.summary: TUM's 'self-reflective' robots use a vision-language-action model that pauses when unsure so a person can demonstrate. Retraining on those moments cut the training needed by up to 20%, and each new skill goes into its own adapter so old ones aren't forgotten.

Here's your day in transhumanism, in 3 minutes flat.
Up to speed! Google DeepMind's AI agents found faster quantum algorithms, and proved every one.
And a rare muscle-wasting disease got its firs t approved drug; patients on it walked faster.
A brain implant gives Mary a voice. With Nvidia, its computer cart should shrink to a box.

On to longevity. In half a million Britons, the dirtiest air came with a quarter more dementia risk.
And a Cambridge study found leukaemia's first mutation often appears before age 20, decades before diagnosis.

Closer to home, after South Australia relaxed medical checks for older drivers, their crash rate actually fell.
On to wellbeing. Across 5,000 singles in 5 countries, feeling free went with feeling happier.
Meanwhile, 1 in 4 students at Bath turned to AI for mental-health support; more among those struggling.
Now, the catch.
Australia's health minister ordered an inquiry into peptides sold online as anti-ageing shortcuts.
And a preprint found top AI models steering robot s often did harm in tests; a safety leash helped.
On the frontier, a drone folds its springy arms to squeeze through gaps half its width.
A fungus that thrives at Chernobyl inspired tiny sphe res that break down a nerve-agent stand-in in minutes.

Faster maths, faster legs, and robots that know when to brake. Now you're up to speed!
Every day, the curve gets a little steeper.
And the future keeps arriving ahead of schedule.
One day, all of this. Tomorrow, probably more.
That's the Transhuman Daily for today.
